passages.t: The nations gathered, and the slave trade judged
passages.happening:
In those days, when God restores the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem, he will gather all the nations to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. ‘There I will enter into judgment against them concerning My people’ (verse 2), whom they scattered among the nations as they divided up his land. They cast lots for his people. They bartered a boy for a prostitute and sold a girl for wine (verse 3).

God turns to Tyre, Sidon and the regions of Philistia (verse 4). They took his silver and gold and carried his treasures off to their temples (verse 5). ‘You sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks, to send them far from their homeland’ (verse 6). God will rouse the captives from the places where they were sold and turn the crime back on those who did it (verse 7). Their own sons and daughters will be sold to the people of Judah, and on to the Sabeans, a distant nation (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 3, chapter 4 in the Hebrew Bible, widens the lens from Judah to the nations. The Day of the LORD, which first threatened Judah through the locusts, now turns against those who have wronged God's people. The words about restoring Judah from captivity can also be translated as restoring its fortunes, a general phrase for the reversal of disaster.

The name Jehoshaphat means the LORD judges, and the valley is a place where God's verdict is given. Tyre and Sidon were the great Phoenician ports on the coast, famous for trade, including trade in people. Philistia was the coastal plain to the southwest. The Greeks were active traders in the eastern Mediterranean from the eighth century BC on, so their mention does not settle Joel's date, though many scholars take it as a sign of a later setting. The Sabeans were the people of Sheba in southern Arabia, whose caravans traded far and wide.

Casting lots was a common way to divide captives after a battle. A boy traded for a prostitute and a girl for wine show how cheaply the slave trade valued human life: children were currency for an evening's pleasures. The word for temples in verse 5 can also mean palaces. Either way, the treasures of God's house had been carried off as trophies.
passages.later: Amos condemns Gaza and Tyre for handing whole populations over to Edom as slaves (Amos 1:6-10), and Ezekiel names Greece among Tyre's partners in trading human beings (Ezekiel 27:13).
passages.hard:
Is this chapter a call for vengeance on other nations?

The chapter is fierce, and readers are right to notice it. Two things shape how it should be read. The judgment is God's, not Judah's: the people are not told to take revenge, and even the summons to war is given to the nations, who come to face God's verdict. And the charges are specific crimes, above all the enslaving and selling of children and the violent seizing of land, which any moral reader sees as grave evils.

Verse 8, where Judah sells the sons and daughters of Tyre and Sidon, is the hardest line. Many interpreters read it as a statement of just repayment in the language of the ancient world, the punishment mirroring the crime, rather than an approval of slavery. Others point out that the prophets elsewhere promise that nations, Egypt and Assyria among them, will one day worship God (Isaiah 19:23-25), and that Joel has just promised the Spirit to all people.

The chapter says that God will not let atrocities stand. It gives no warrant for hatred of any people, then or now, and it is not a statement about any modern nation or conflict.
passages.asks: God sees children who were sold for a night's pleasure, and he names it. Ask who is treated as cheap in your own world, and whether you have looked away. And ask how you can long for justice without longing for revenge.

passages.t: Plowshares into swords, and the valley of decision
passages.happening:
Proclaim it among the nations: prepare for war, rouse the warriors (verse 9). ‘Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears’ (verse 10), and let the weak call themselves strong. Let the nations come quickly and gather in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, ‘for there I will sit down to judge all the nations on every side’ (verse 12).

‘Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe’ (verse 13). The winepress is full and the vats overflow, because their wickedness is great. “Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision! For the Day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision” (verse 14). The sun, moon and stars go dark (verse 15). ‘The LORD will roar from Zion and raise His voice from Jerusalem’ (verse 16), and heaven and earth tremble. But the LORD will be a refuge for his people.
passages.hearers:
The chapter is a courtroom and a battlefield in one. After the charges comes a mocking summons to war, in which the weak are told to call themselves strong. Verse 10 turns a famous promise inside out. Isaiah and Micah foresaw nations beating swords into plowshares. Here, before that peace can come, the nations must face judgment, and they are told to do the opposite.

The harvest pictures come from the grain and grape seasons. The sickle cut ripe grain. Grapes were trampled by foot in a winepress, a flat rock basin from which juice ran into a lower vat. An overflowing vat was usually a sign of plenty. Here it pictures wickedness ripe for judgment.

The valley of decision is the same valley, the place where God gives his verdict. Verse 16 shares its opening line with Amos 1:2. The God who roars is also a refuge.
passages.later: Isaiah and Micah promised the reverse: ‘They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks’ (Isaiah 2:4; Micah 4:3). Amos opens with the same roar from Zion (Amos 1:2).
passages.asks: The nations are told to call themselves strong before God, and it does them no good. Ask where you have trusted your own strength. And the same God who roars is a refuge. Ask how you can hold both of those together.

passages.happening:
‘Then you will know that I am the LORD your God, who dwells in Zion, My holy mountain’ (verse 17). Jerusalem will be holy.

‘And in that day the mountains will drip with sweet wine, and the hills will flow with milk’ (verse 18). All the streams of Judah will run with water, and a spring will flow from the house of the LORD to water the Valley of Acacias. Egypt and Edom will become desolate because of the violence done to the people of Judah and the innocent blood they shed (verse 19). But Judah will be inhabited forever (verse 20). The book ends, ‘For the LORD dwells in Zion’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The book that began with stripped vines and dry streams ends with mountains dripping with wine and streams full of water. Joel's arc runs from disaster to restoration, and God is no longer distant: he dwells in Zion.

The Valley of Acacias was probably a dry wadi, a streambed that flows only in the rainy season. Acacias grow in dry ground, so a spring from the temple watering that valley promises life where there had been none.

Egypt and Edom had both shed Judah's blood. Egypt invaded under Pharaoh Shishak in the tenth century BC, and Pharaoh Neco killed King Josiah in 609 BC. Edom was remembered for its hostility when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. Which events Joel has in mind depends on his date, which is still debated. The charge is violence and innocent blood, and the verdict is God's.
passages.later: Ezekiel saw water flowing from under the temple and giving life wherever it went (Ezekiel 47:1-12), and Zechariah saw living water flowing out from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8). Obadiah tells of Edom's part in Jerusalem's fall (Obadiah 10-14).
passages.asks: The last words of Joel are that the LORD dwells in Zion. Ask what difference it makes that the book ends with God's presence, not only with the land's harvest. And ask where you need a spring of life to run through dry ground.
